free_tier.stated: no service and no account; a fork of wireguard-go with a WebSocket transport

egress.terms: not applicable; the software states no volume; ingress: tcp

tooling: go build; TLS certificates for the server side
chaining: composes with any host where the operator can run the forked binary at both ends; no CDN is documented as tested.
binding_note: both ends must run the fork and the server needs a TLS certificate; there is no hosted service to attach to
reliability_note: client defaults to skipping certificate verification (WG_WS_INSECURE=1); no releases, one author
confidence_note: the repository has no releases and no stars, so the rung cannot rise without a build and a measured run

evidence.proved: "a fork of wireguard-go with added WebSocket transport support ... Fully compatible with standard wg and wg-quick tools"
WG_WS=1 with WG_WS_CERT_FILE on the server and WG_WS_INSECURE=1 on the client; clients connect to wss://host:port/ws

notes: The interesting property is that the transport change happens inside the WireGuard implementation, so the interface and the configuration stay standard: this is the closest thing to a wrapper that a .conf-only router could accept, if the router ran the fork. It does not, so in practice the fork must run on a Linux host at both ends. Zero stars and no releases make it a reference for the approach rather than a deployment.

extras.wg_detail: "Fully compatible with standard wg and wg-quick tools"; WG_WS=1 switches the transport and the peer endpoint stays host:port
extras.volume_stated: not applicable; the software states no volume
extras.transit_note: over a websocket between two hosts running the fork
extras.hosting_requirement: two hosts running the fork, the server one with a TLS certificate
